title: Shalva's Illusion of Vasudeva's Death
story:
In the middle of the battle, a man came running toward Krishna's chariot, weeping and calling his name.

Krishna had hurried home to this war. Omens had reached him in the midst of his cousin Yudhishthira's great sacrifice, and he had found his own sky occupied: while he was away, Shalva, king of Saubha, had brought his iron flying city down upon the coast. Since Krishna's return the two had fought a running duel across the sea — Shalva raining iron javelins, flaming lances and heavy clubs from his height, Krishna cutting each one into two or three pieces before it could reach him, so that the sea below rained splinters. Then the duel had reached its strangest moment. Krishna hurled his mace at the king with a force that would have felled a mountain; when the mace came spinning back to his hand, the sky where Shalva had stood was empty, and his war-cries came from everywhere and nowhere at once.

Now the weeping man was stumbling among the chariots, his clothes torn, his voice broken. 'Krishna, Krishna, mighty-armed one!' he cried. 'Your father — you who love your father!' He said he had come from Dwaraka, though he gave no name, and in the press of battle Krishna did not think to ask for one. Shalva, the man sobbed, had broken into the city and carried off Vasudeva, Krishna's own father, like an animal; the tyrant held him now, and only Krishna could save him. It was easy to believe: behind them lay Dwaraka, undefended while Krishna fought.

And then Shalva himself stood before Krishna, gripping an old man dressed in Vasudeva's robes. 'Here is your father!' Shalva shouted, holding the captive up for all to see. 'The man you live for! Save him, if you can!' And before Krishna could move, Shalva's sword came down, and the old man's head fell into the dust.

For one moment — the old telling is careful about this — Krishna let himself be wholly human, and his face was any son's face who has watched his father die. He was not thinking of war, or sorcery, or the city in the sky; he was thinking only of the old man in the dust. The grief came over him like a wave, and for a second his eyes lost the battle.

Then he looked again.

There was no messenger. There was no body, no head, no blood — only the sky, and Saubha wheeling in it, and Shalva's laughter ringing down. It had all been maya: sorcery, the art of making what is not real seem real. The grief left Krishna's face as mist leaves a field at sunrise, and the calm that replaced it was more terrible than any anger. His father was safe; the death had never happened. Shalva had staked the war on the one blow that could shake him, and the blow had not landed.

Krishna turned back to the sky where Saubha drifted, his face utterly calm. The sorcery had spent itself; nothing it could show him now would move him. He raised his bow, and the real battle began.
reflection: Krishna's moment of grief is the hinge of the scene: the sorcery works, and then it fails. The Bhagavata's sages note that bewilderment cannot truly touch him, but the story lets the human mood stand first — a son's grief worn for an instant and then seen through, which is what makes the recovery feel like a return to himself.
tradition_note: The Mahabharata tells the same scene with a stronger effect: Krishna swoons and the bow Sharanga slips from his hand before he recognizes the illusion. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana, where his bewilderment lasts only a moment.
next_story_tease: But Shalva's flying city still wheeled above Dwaraka, and the war was not yet over.
hero_scene: On the battlefield below Dwaraka, Shalva holds up the hooded figure of the illusory Vasudeva and raises his sword while Krishna stands in his chariot, grief and recognition crossing his face in the same instant, and the flying city Saubha wheels in the sky above.

Shalva holding up the illusory Vasudeva and raising his sword
the weeping messenger stumbling among the chariots
the severed head of the illusory father falling into the dust
the flying city Saubha wheeling in the sky above Dwaraka
the sea below raining splinters of shattered weapons
